topic: Principles of Nutrition, Proximate Analysis & Nutrient Metabolism
questionText: When comparing the chemical composition of the mammalian body with green pasture plants on a dry matter basis, which contrast is accurate?
options: Both plant and animal dry matter maintain an identical 1:1 ratio of crude protein to nitrogen-free extract across all growth stages
Animals contain mainly protein and fat with <1% carbohydrate, whereas plants contain 70–80% structural and soluble carbohydrates
Animals store over 45% of their dry matter as hepatic and muscular glycogen, whereas plants store energy chiefly as triglycerides
Plants contain over 55% crude protein and negligible cell-wall fiber compared to the high structural carbohydrate content of livestock
explanation: In the animal body, carbohydrates (glycogen and blood glucose) constitute less than 1% of dry weight, whereas proteins and lipids dominate. Conversely, plant dry matter consists of 70–80% carbohydrates (cellulose, hemicellulose, starch, and sugars).

topic: Principles of Nutrition, Proximate Analysis & Nutrient Metabolism
questionText: As a growing meat animal matures and undergoes fattening from birth to adulthood, how does the composition of its fat-free empty body change?
options: Water percentage rises steadily with age, while the protein-to-ash ratio drops from 80:20 in neonates to 40:60 in mature cattle
Crude protein concentration doubles on a wet-tissue basis, while total body lipid drops below 3% of empty body weight at maturity
Total body mineral ash expands to replace adipose depots, causing the water-to-protein ratio to increase exponentially in adults
Water percentage drops as fat content rises, while fat-free dry matter retains a constant ~80:20 protein-to-ash ratio
explanation: Body water and body fat are inversely correlated: as fat increases from ~4% in neonates to >30% in fattened adults, water falls from ~75% to ~50%. However, on a fat-free dry matter basis, the ratio of protein to ash remains remarkably constant at roughly 80:20 (4:1).

topic: Principles of Nutrition, Proximate Analysis & Nutrient Metabolism
questionText: Complete mitochondrial oxidation of 100 grams each of pure dietary fat, starch, and protein yields approximately what respective amounts of metabolic water?
options: 107.0 g from fat, 55.6 g from starch, and 41.3 g from protein during aerobic cellular respiration
55.6 g from fat, 107.0 g from starch, and 82.4 g from protein during complete aerobic cellular respiration
41.3 g from fat, 55.6 g from starch, and 107.0 g from protein during complete aerobic cellular respiration
88.5 g from fat, 74.2 g from starch, and 62.5 g from protein during complete aerobic cellular respiration
explanation: Because fatty acids have a high hydrogen-to-oxygen ratio and require high oxygen uptake for complete oxidation, 100 g of fat yields ~107 g of metabolic water, compared to ~55.6 g from 100 g of starch/carbohydrate and ~41.3 g from 100 g of protein.

topic: Principles of Nutrition, Proximate Analysis & Nutrient Metabolism
questionText: Why does a high-protein ration increase an animal's net drinking water requirement despite generating 41.3 g of metabolic water per 100 g of protein oxidized?
options: Ruminal deamination of amino acids converts all intracellular metabolic water into gaseous methane lost during eructation
Dietary amino acids directly inhibit hypothalamic vasopressin release and induce severe renal diabetes insipidus in livestock
Renal clearance of resulting urea and sulfate loads demands obligatory urinary water exceeding the metabolic water formed
Abomasal and pancreatic proteases consume ten times more water molecules during peptide bond hydrolysis than amylase digestion
explanation: Catabolism of excess protein produces urea (in mammals) and sulfates/phosphates that require substantial obligatory urinary water for renal excretion, resulting in a net water deficit per gram of protein oxidized compared to carbohydrates or fats.

topic: Principles of Nutrition, Proximate Analysis & Nutrient Metabolism
questionText: Which nitrogen excretion adaptation enables domestic poultry to conserve significantly more body water during protein catabolism than mammals?
options: Complete absence of glomerular filtration in avian nephrons coupled with cutaneous evaporation of gaseous ammonia across skin
Direct storage of crystalline urea inside the avian ceca for subsequent bacterial resynthesis without any renal clearance
Excretion of nitrogen chiefly as insoluble uric acid rather than soluble urea, minimizing obligatory urinary water loss
Hepatic conversion of excess dietary amino acids into subcutaneous wax esters that release 200 g of water per 100 g oxidized
explanation: Birds are uricotelic; uric acid precipitates out of solution in the urodeum/cloaca as a semi-solid white paste, allowing nitrogen excretion with minimal obligatory water loss, whereas ureotelic mammals require large volumes of water to excrete soluble urea.

topic: Principles of Nutrition, Proximate Analysis & Nutrient Metabolism
questionText: As forage grasses advance in physiological maturity from the vegetative leafy stage to flowering and seed setting, which compositional shift occurs?
options: Total mineral ash and silica disappear from the stem fraction as hemicellulose converts into water-soluble fructan polymers
Crude protein and cell solubles decline progressively while neutral detergent fiber and lignin concentrations increase
Digestible organic matter increases linearly because secondary cell-wall lignification enhances ruminal bacterial attachment
Acid detergent lignin and cellulose decline sharply while soluble cytoplasmic protein and beta-carotene concentrations double
explanation: During plant maturation, the leaf-to-stem ratio falls and secondary cell walls thicken and lignify. Consequently, Crude Protein (CP) and soluble carbohydrates decline, while NDF, ADF, and indigestible lignin (ADL) increase, lowering digestibility and intake.

topic: Principles of Nutrition, Proximate Analysis & Nutrient Metabolism
questionText: Under thermoneutral conditions, voluntary free drinking water intake in adult non-lactating cattle is most closely proportional to which dietary parameter?
options: Total dry matter intake, averaging approximately 3 to 4 liters of water per kilogram of dry matter consumed
Dietary ether extract percentage alone, independent of total dry matter consumption or environmental humidity
Concentration of fat-soluble vitamins A, D, and E provided in the daily trace mineral supplement premix
Total dietary crude fiber content multiplied by the biological value of the supplemental bypass protein source
explanation: Voluntary water intake is strongly correlated with Dry Matter Intake (DMI); adult cattle in thermoneutral environments consume approximately 3 to 4 liters of water per kg of DM intake, plus ~0.87 liters of water per kg of milk secreted during lactation.

topic: Principles of Nutrition, Proximate Analysis & Nutrient Metabolism
questionText: Why is toluene distillation preferred over standard hot-air oven drying at 100–105°C when determining the dry matter content of fermented corn or grass silage?
options: Cellulose and acid detergent lignin sublime directly into gas at 100°C inside a standard laboratory convection oven
Inorganic silica and calcium carbonate decompose into carbon dioxide gas at 102°C during standard gravimetric drying
Atmospheric nitrogen condenses onto the aluminum dish during heating and artificially inflates the recovered dry matter
Oven drying volatilizes short-chain fatty acids, lactic acid, and ammonia with water, underestimating dry matter
explanation: In fermented silages, oven heating at 100–105°C drives off volatile organic acids (acetic, propionic, butyric), alcohols, and ammonia along with moisture, overestimating water content and underestimating true Dry Matter (DM) by 2–8%. Toluene distillation accurately captures only water.

topic: Principles of Nutrition, Proximate Analysis & Nutrient Metabolism
questionText: The classical Weende system of proximate feed analysis was developed in 1860 at the Weende Experiment Station in Germany by which pair of scientists?
options: Peter J. Van Soest and R.H. Wine at the USDA Beltsville agricultural research center
Wilhelm Henneberg and Friedrich Stohmann at the Göttingen-Weende experiment station
J.M.A. Tilley and R.A. Terry at the Grassland Research Institute in Hurley, England
Oskar Kellner and Henry Prentiss Armsby during their respiration calorimetry trials
explanation: Wilhelm Henneberg and Friedrich Stohmann developed the Weende proximate analysis scheme in 1860–1865 at Weende near Göttingen, partitioning feedstuffs into Moisture, Crude Protein, Ether Extract, Crude Fiber, Total Ash, and Nitrogen-Free Extract.

topic: Principles of Nutrition, Proximate Analysis & Nutrient Metabolism
questionText: While general feeds use the Kjeldahl conversion factor of 6.25 (16% N), what specific nitrogen-to-protein conversion factors apply to milk protein and wheat grain protein?
options: 6.38 for milk protein (15.67% N) and 5.70 for wheat grain protein (17.5% N)
5.55 for milk protein (18.00% N) and 6.00 for wheat grain protein (16.67% N)
6.25 for milk protein (16.00% N) and 7.50 for wheat grain protein (13.33% N)
5.70 for milk protein (17.50% N) and 6.38 for wheat grain protein (15.67% N)
explanation: Pure dairy proteins (casein and lactalbumin) contain ~15.67% nitrogen, giving a specific Kjeldahl factor of 100 / 15.67 = 6.38. Wheat gluten proteins (gliadin and glutenin) are rich in glutamine and contain ~17.5% nitrogen, giving a factor of 100 / 17.5 = 5.70.

topic: Principles of Nutrition, Proximate Analysis & Nutrient Metabolism
questionText: During the digestion step of Kjeldahl nitrogen estimation, feed is boiled with concentrated $H_2SO_4$ in the presence of anhydrous $K_2SO_4$ and $CuSO_4$ (in a 9:1 or 10:1 ratio). What are the respective roles of $K_2SO_4$ and $CuSO_4$?
options: Potassium sulfate neutralizes sulfuric acid to release free ammonia gas, while copper sulfate prevents nitrate volatilization
Potassium sulfate precipitates true protein away from urea, while copper sulfate serves as the pH indicator during acid titration
Potassium sulfate raises the boiling point of sulfuric acid (~380°C), while copper sulfate acts as an oxidation catalyst
Potassium sulfate reduces ammonium ions to elemental nitrogen, while copper sulfate absorbs evolved sulfur dioxide fumes
explanation: In Kjeldahl digestion, concentrated $H_2SO_4$ converts organic nitrogen into ammonium sulfate $(NH_4)_2SO_4$. Anhydrous potassium sulfate ($K_2SO_4$) or sodium sulfate elevates the boiling point of $H_2SO_4$ from ~337°C to 370–400°C, while copper sulfate ($CuSO_4$) catalyzes oxidation of organic matter.

topic: Principles of Nutrition, Proximate Analysis & Nutrient Metabolism
questionText: In the micro-Kjeldahl distillation step, liberated ammonia gas ($NH_3$) is trapped in 2–4% boric acid ($H_3BO_3$) containing Tashiro's mixed indicator. How is the captured nitrogen quantified?
options: By gravimetric precipitation with barium chloride solution followed by ignition in a muffle furnace at 600°C for four hours
By colorimetric oxidation with potassium permanganate in 1 N sulfuric acid until a permanent purple endpoint is reached
By back-titration against standard 0.5 N sodium hydroxide after adding an excess of concentrated nitric acid to the flask
By direct titration of the ammonium borate complex against standard acid ($0.1\text{ N } H_2SO_4$ or $HCl$) to the endpoint
explanation: Ammonia reacts with boric acid ($NH_3 + H_3BO_3 \to NH_4^+ + H_2BO_3^-$); the resulting dihydrogen borate ion is a strong enough conjugate base to be titrated directly with standard $0.1\text{ N } H_2SO_4$ or $HCl$ using Tashiro's indicator (methyl red + methylene blue), eliminating back-titration.

topic: Principles of Nutrition, Proximate Analysis & Nutrient Metabolism
questionText: To separate and quantify 'True Protein' from Non-Protein Nitrogen (NPN) in green forages prior to Kjeldahl digestion (Barnstein's method), which precipitating reagent is classically used?
options: Cetyl trimethyl ammonium bromide (CTAB) dissolved in 1.0 N sulfuric acid solution
Anhydrous petroleum ether (boiling range 40–60°C) in a continuous Soxhlet apparatus
Stutzer's reagent (alkaline cupric hydroxide) or 10% trichloroacetic acid (TCA)
1.25% sulfuric acid followed sequentially by 1.25% sodium hydroxide for 30 minutes each
explanation: In Stutzer's or Barnstein's method, boiling the aqueous feed suspension with copper sulfate and sodium hydroxide forms insoluble cupric hydroxide $Cu(OH)_2$ (Stutzer's reagent)—or treating with 10% Trichloroacetic acid (TCA)/tungstic acid—which precipitates True Protein while soluble NPN (amides, free amino acids, urea, nitrates) passes into the filtrate.

topic: Principles of Nutrition, Proximate Analysis & Nutrient Metabolism
questionText: Why must a feed sample be dried to a moisture-free state before conducting Soxhlet extraction with petroleum ether (boiling point 40–60°C) for Ether Extract determination?
options: Water coats feed particles to block non-polar solvent entry and co-extracts soluble sugars, urea, and lactic acid
Traces of water react explosively with boiling petroleum ether to form insoluble lignin polymers inside the siphon tube
Moisture hydrolyzes neutral triglycerides into insoluble calcium soaps that cannot dissolve in organic solvents
Water causes chlorophyll and carotenoid pigments to sublime out of the condenser and lower the flask weight
explanation: Moisture forms a hydrophilic film over feed particles that prevents hydrophobic ether penetration; moreover, if diethyl ether containing water is used, water-soluble non-lipids (sugars, urea, organic acids) leach into the extract and falsely inflate the Ether Extract percentage.

topic: Principles of Nutrition, Proximate Analysis & Nutrient Metabolism
questionText: Which non-triglyceride, lipid-soluble compounds are co-extracted into the Ether Extract (EE) fraction of leafy green roughages, making forage EE much lower in true caloric value than oilseed EE?
options: Free amino acids, purine and pyrimidine bases, betaine, and water-soluble B-complex vitamins in cytoplasm
Chlorophyll, carotenoids, cuticular plant waxes, sterols, phospholipids, and fat-soluble vitamins
Phytic acid, soluble potassium oxalates, biogenic silica, and acid-insoluble ash complexes in stem tissues
Pectins, beta-glucans, fructans, arabinoxylans, and water-soluble Maillard browning polymers in cell walls
explanation: In green leafy forages, up to 40–50% of the Soxhlet Ether Extract consists of non-glyceride ether-soluble substances—especially chlorophyll, xanthophylls, carotenes, cuticular waxes, and sterols—which are poorly digestible and yield far less usable energy than true seed triglycerides.

topic: Principles of Nutrition, Proximate Analysis & Nutrient Metabolism
questionText: In the Weende determination of Crude Fiber (CF), the moisture-free and fat-free feed residue is boiled sequentially for 30 minutes each in which specific pair of solutions?
options: 1.0 N sulfuric acid containing 2% CTAB detergent followed by washing with acetone and diethyl ether
72% w/w sulfuric acid ($H_2SO_4$) for 3 hours followed by neutral sodium lauryl sulfate solution at pH 7.0
10% w/v hydrochloric acid ($HCl$) followed by 40% w/v potassium hydroxide ($KOH$) under steam autoclaving
1.25% w/v (0.255 N) sulfuric acid ($H_2SO_4$) followed by 1.25% w/v (0.313 N) sodium hydroxide ($NaOH$)
explanation: Weende Crude Fiber is determined by refluxing the fat-free dry residue sequentially for 30 minutes in dilute acid ($1.25\%\text{ w/v } H_2SO_4$, 0.255 N) and 30 minutes in dilute alkali ($1.25\%\text{ w/v } NaOH$, 0.313 N), then drying, weighing, and ashing at 550–600°C to subtract mineral ash.

topic: Principles of Nutrition, Proximate Analysis & Nutrient Metabolism
questionText: What is the principal chemical limitation of the Weende Crude Fiber (CF) and Nitrogen-Free Extract (NFE) system when evaluating fibrous ruminant roughages?
options: Total mineral ash is counted twice in both the Crude Fiber residue and the NFE formula, causing proximate fractions to sum to 120%
Boiling in 1.25% NaOH dissolves much of the lignin and hemicellulose into NFE, making CF sometimes more digestible than NFE
Boiling in 1.25% sulfuric acid completely hydrolyzes crystalline cellulose into glucose, leaving only silica in the Crude Fiber fraction
Cereal starch and sucrose are completely insoluble in boiling dilute acid and alkali, causing all grain starch to be measured as Crude Fiber
explanation: Because boiling $1.25\%\text{ NaOH}$ solubilizes up to 50–80% of indigestible lignin and a major share of hemicellulose, these cell-wall components are lost from Crude Fiber and accrue by difference into NFE. Consequently, for ~25–30% of straws and hays, CF digestibility artificially exceeds NFE digestibility.

topic: Principles of Nutrition, Proximate Analysis & Nutrient Metabolism
questionText: When the Total Ash obtained from a muffle furnace (550–600°C) is boiled in dilute hydrochloric acid (10% HCl) and filtered through ashless paper, what does the undissolved residue represent?
options: Bioavailable macrominerals including calcium phosphate, magnesium oxide, and soluble potassium carbonate salts
Organic phytate phosphorus and calcium oxalate crystals that remain intact after 600°C muffle incineration
Acid-Insoluble Ash (AIA), consisting mainly of biogenic plant silica ($SiO_2$) and sand/soil contamination
Volatile trace elements such as selenium, iodine, and chloride that resist muffle furnace ignition at 600°C
explanation: Boiling Total Ash in dilute HCl dissolves physiological mineral salts, leaving Acid-Insoluble Ash (AIA), which consists of plant silica ($SiO_2$) and extraneous sand/soil. BIS standards cap AIA (e.g., max 2.5–4.0% in cattle feeds) to detect sand/husk adulteration, and AIA is also used as an internal digestibility marker.

topic: Principles of Nutrition, Proximate Analysis & Nutrient Metabolism
questionText: In the Van Soest detergent system of fiber analysis, which specific surfactant and pH conditions are utilized to extract Neutral Detergent Fiber (NDF)?
options: Sodium lauryl sulfate with disodium EDTA in a borate-phosphate buffer at neutral pH 7.0
Sodium deoxycholate bile salt dissolved in 72% concentrated sulfuric acid solution at 20°C
Tween-80 non-ionic surfactant dissolved in 1.25% aqueous sodium hydroxide solution at pH 13.0
Cetyl trimethyl ammonium bromide (CTAB) dissolved in 1.0 N sulfuric acid solution at pH < 1.0
explanation: Van Soest's Neutral Detergent Solution uses the anionic surfactant Sodium Lauryl Sulfate (30 g/L) with disodium EDTA (to chelate calcium and remove pectins), sodium borate, disodium phosphate, and 2-ethoxyethanol buffered at pH 6.9–7.1.

topic: Principles of Nutrition, Proximate Analysis & Nutrient Metabolism
questionText: In the official AOAC assay for amylase-treated Neutral Detergent Fiber (aNDF), why are heat-stable $\alpha$-amylase and sodium sulfite ($Na_2SO_3$) added during boiling?
options: Alpha-amylase precipitates soluble pectins into NDF, while sodium sulfite oxidizes cellulose into acid-insoluble lignin
Alpha-amylase dissolves crystalline hemicellulose into xylose, while sodium sulfite protects carotene from oxidation
Both reagents are added solely to neutralize the 1.0 N sulfuric acid used during the neutral detergent digestion step
Alpha-amylase hydrolyzes gelatinized starch that clogs filters, while sodium sulfite cleaves protein disulfide bonds
explanation: In starchy concentrates and corn silage, boiling gelatinizes starch which clogs fritted glass filters and inflates NDF; heat-stable $\alpha$-amylase removes this starch. Sodium sulfite ($Na_2SO_3$) cleaves disulfide ($-S-S-$) linkages to solubilize heat-denatured and keratinous proteins.

topic: Principles of Nutrition, Proximate Analysis & Nutrient Metabolism
questionText: Which structural plant cell-wall polysaccharide (abundant in legume leaves, sugar beet pulp, and citrus pulp) is completely dissolved by EDTA in Neutral Detergent Solution and excluded from NDF?
options: Crystalline beta-1,4-glucan cellulose microfibrils embedded within the secondary plant cell wall
Pectin (polygalacturonic acid of the middle lamella, rapidly fermented in the rumen)
Phenylpropanoid core lignin polymers synthesized from coniferyl and sinapyl alcohols
Hemicellulose (beta-1,4-xylan and arabinoxylan chains cross-linked with ferulic acid esters)
explanation: Pectin in the intercellular middle lamella is bound to calcium ($Ca^{2+}$). Disodium EDTA in the Neutral Detergent solution chelates $Ca^{2+}$ and extracts pectin into the Neutral Detergent Solubles (NDS) fraction; nutritionally, pectin ferments rapidly and completely in the rumen without generating lactic acid.

topic: Principles of Nutrition, Proximate Analysis & Nutrient Metabolism
questionText: What is the exact chemical composition of the Acid Detergent Solution used by Van Soest to isolate Acid Detergent Fiber (ADF)?
options: 30 g/L Sodium lauryl sulfate dissolved in 1.25% w/v hydrochloric acid ($HCl$) solution
50 g/L Benzalkonium chloride dissolved in 72% (24 N) concentrated sulfuric acid ($H_2SO_4$)
15 g/L Triton X-100 surfactant dissolved in 0.255 N glacial acetic acid at pH 4.5
20 g/L Cetyl trimethyl ammonium bromide (CTAB) in 1.0 N sulfuric acid ($H_2SO_4$)
explanation: Acid Detergent Solution consists of 2% w/v (20 g/L) Cetyl Trimethyl Ammonium Bromide (CTAB, a quaternary ammonium cationic detergent) dissolved in $1.0\text{ N } H_2SO_4$ (49 g/L). Refluxing for 1 hour hydrolyzes hemicellulose, leaving cellulose, lignin, cutin, and silica as ADF.

topic: Principles of Nutrition, Proximate Analysis & Nutrient Metabolism
questionText: In practical dairy ration formulation, how do Neutral Detergent Fiber (NDF) and Acid Detergent Fiber (ADF) differ in the primary animal response each fraction predicts?
options: NDF best predicts physical rumen fill and voluntary Dry Matter Intake, whereas ADF best predicts forage digestibility
ADF predicts physical rumen fill and chewing time, whereas NDF predicts only the total mineral ash content of hay
NDF predicts only abomasal protein bioavailability, whereas ADF predicts voluntary water intake and ruminal pH
Neither fraction correlates with intake or digestibility because lignin dissolves completely in both detergent solutions
explanation: Because NDF encompasses the entire slowly-fermenting structural cell wall (hemicellulose + cellulose + lignin), it governs physical rumen fill and inversely predicts voluntary Dry Matter Intake ($DMI\%\text{ BW} \approx 120/\%NDF$). ADF (cellulose + lignin) correlates inversely with forage digestibility and TDN/NE.

topic: Principles of Nutrition, Proximate Analysis & Nutrient Metabolism
questionText: In the Van Soest detergent system, how is Acid Detergent Lignin (ADL) isolated from the Acid Detergent Fiber (ADF) residue in the standard Klason-type procedure?
options: By extracting the ADF residue in a Soxhlet apparatus with boiling petroleum ether and acetone for 6 hours
By boiling the ADF residue in 1.25% sodium hydroxide for 30 minutes to dissolve cellulose while leaving lignin intact
By treating the ADF residue with cold 72% sulfuric acid for 3 hours to dissolve cellulose, then ashing
By incubating the ADF residue with pepsin and 0.1 N hydrochloric acid at 39°C for 48 hours to digest beta-glucans
explanation: Treating the ADF residue with cold $72\%\text{ w/w } H_2SO_4$ for 3 hours dissolves crystalline cellulose, leaving Acid Detergent Lignin (ADL), cutin, and acid-insoluble silica. Subsequent ashing in a muffle furnace burns off organic lignin so silica weight can be subtracted.

topic: Principles of Nutrition, Proximate Analysis & Nutrient Metabolism
questionText: Why is plant lignin completely indigestible within the strictly anaerobic environment of the reticulorumen?
options: Lignin is a phenylpropanoid polymer linked by C-C and ether bonds whose cleavage requires molecular oxygen
Lignin consists of long-chain saturated wax esters that precipitate instantly as insoluble calcium soaps in rumen fluid
Lignin is a beta-1,4-galacturonic acid polysaccharide chelated with magnesium ions that competitively inhibits bacterial cellulase
Lignin is an alpha-1,6-glucosamine polymer identical to insect chitin that cannot be hydrated at normal ruminal pH 6.5
explanation: Lignin is not a carbohydrate; it is a complex hydrophobic polymer of phenylpropane alcohols (coniferyl, sinapyl, and p-coumaryl alcohols) linked by stable C-C and aryl-ether bonds. Enzymatic depolymerization of lignin requires aerobic $O_2$-dependent peroxidases and laccases (as in white-rot fungi) and cannot occur in the anaerobic rumen.

topic: Principles of Nutrition, Proximate Analysis & Nutrient Metabolism
questionText: When high-moisture hay or low-moisture haylage overheats (>55–60°C) in storage, the non-enzymatic Maillard reaction binds amino acids to sugar carbonyls. Which laboratory fraction quantifies this heat-damaged, indigestible protein?
options: Urease Activity Index (UAI) measured by pH elevation after buffered urea incubation
Alkaline Cupric Hydroxide Soluble Nitrogen (ACHSN) measured by Stutzer's precipitation
Acid Detergent Insoluble Nitrogen (ADIN) measured by Kjeldahl analysis of ADF
Neutral Detergent Soluble Nitrogen (NDSN) measured in the neutral detergent filtrate
explanation: Maillard polymer complexes (melanoidins) formed between reducing sugars and the $\varepsilon$-amino group of lysine are insoluble in Acid Detergent solution and indigestible in the GI tract. Measuring nitrogen in the ADF residue (ADIN or ADF-CP) diagnoses heat damage when ADIN exceeds 10–12% of total N.

topic: Principles of Nutrition, Proximate Analysis & Nutrient Metabolism
questionText: In modern dairy nutrition (CNCPS / NRC), how is the percentage of Non-Fiber Carbohydrates (NFC) calculated on a dry matter basis?
options: $NFC\% = 100 - (\%CF + \%ADF + \%Moisture)$
$NFC\% = (\%CP \times 6.25) + (\%EE \times 2.25) - \%Ash$
$NFC\% = (\%NDF - \%ADF) + \%ADL + \%Ash$
explanation: Unlike Weende NFE which subtracts Crude Fiber, Non-Fiber Carbohydrates (NFC) is calculated on a dry matter basis by subtracting Neutral Detergent Fiber: $NFC\% = 100 - (\%NDF + \%CP + \%EE + \%Ash)$. NFC includes starch, simple sugars, fructans, organic acids, and pectins.

topic: Principles of Nutrition, Proximate Analysis & Nutrient Metabolism
questionText: A tropical grass hay analyzed on a Dry Matter basis contains 68% NDF, 42% ADF, 8% ADL, and 3% Acid-Insoluble Silica. What are the respective percentages of Hemicellulose and true Cellulose?
options: 60% Hemicellulose and 39% true Cellulose on a dry matter basis
26% Hemicellulose and 31% true Cellulose on a dry matter basis
26% Hemicellulose and 34% true Cellulose on a dry matter basis
42% Hemicellulose and 26% true Cellulose on a dry matter basis
explanation: $Hemicellulose = NDF - ADF = 68\% - 42\% = 26\%$. Since $ADF$ (42%) comprises Cellulose + Lignin (8%) + Acid-insoluble Silica (3%), true $Cellulose = ADF - (ADL + Silica) = 42\% - (8\% + 3\%) = 31\%$.

topic: Principles of Nutrition, Proximate Analysis & Nutrient Metabolism
questionText: Why can ruminants derive up to 70% of their caloric requirements from structural beta-1,4-cellulose, whereas monogastric mammals cannot digest cellulose in the small intestine?
options: Bovine pancreatic juice contains a unique ruminant beta-amylase that cleaves crystalline cellulose inside the duodenum
The bovine abomasum secretes hydrochloric acid at pH 0.5 which chemically hydrolyzes beta-1,4-glucosidic bonds without enzymes
Symbiotic rumen microbes secrete beta-1,4-cellulase complexes, whereas vertebrate genomes lack cellulase genes
Ruminant parotid saliva contains high levels of endogenous cellulase secreted during cud mastication and rumination
explanation: No vertebrate animal possesses a gene encoding cellulase to cleave $\beta(1\to 4)$ glycosidic bonds. Ruminants depend on symbiotic anaerobic bacteria (`Fibrobacter succinogenes`, `Ruminococcus albus`, `R. flavefaciens`), protozoa, and chytrid fungi that produce extracellular cellulosomes.

topic: Principles of Nutrition, Proximate Analysis & Nutrient Metabolism
questionText: Because over 90% of dietary soluble carbohydrates are fermented to Volatile Fatty Acids (VFAs) in the rumen, how does a high-yielding dairy cow meet her massive glucose requirement for milk lactose synthesis?
options: Active sodium-glucose cotransport (SGLT1) of unfermented dietary cellulose monomers across the omasal epithelium
Direct conversion of ruminal acetate and butyrate into glucose via the glyoxylate pathway inside bovine hepatocytes
Direct substitution of beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate for lactose inside the Golgi apparatus of mammary alveoli
Continuous hepatic gluconeogenesis from ruminal propionate along with glucogenic amino acids, lactate, and glycerol
explanation: Ruminants absorb negligible dietary glucose from the gut and rely on continuous hepatic gluconeogenesis. Ruminal propionate ($C_3$, converted via propionyl-CoA and Vitamin $B_{12}$-dependent methylmalonyl-CoA mutase to succinyl-CoA) provides 50–60% of glucose carbon, while acetate ($C_2$) and butyrate ($C_4$) cannot yield net glucose.

topic: Principles of Nutrition, Proximate Analysis & Nutrient Metabolism
questionText: How does the enzymatic and ionic composition of ruminant parotid saliva differ from that of monogastric omnivores such as swine?
options: Ruminant saliva contains high concentrations of bile salts and pancreatic lipase to emulsify forage galactolipids in the mouth
Ruminant saliva lacks alpha-amylase (ptyalin) and is heavily buffered with sodium bicarbonate and phosphate (pH 8.2)
Ruminant saliva contains ten times higher salivary alpha-amylase activity than pig saliva to hydrolyze roughage cellulose
Ruminant saliva is strongly acidic (pH 3.5) and rich in pepsinogen to initiate protein hydrolysis during rumination
explanation: Ruminant saliva (100–190 L/day in cattle) completely lacks salivary $\alpha$-amylase (ptyalin); instead, it is an alkaline (pH 8.1–8.4), isotonic solution rich in sodium bicarbonate (~125 mEq/L), phosphate (~25 mEq/L), mucin, and recycled urea to buffer ruminal VFAs.

topic: Principles of Nutrition, Proximate Analysis & Nutrient Metabolism
questionText: How does the predominant lipid class in green pasture leaves differ chemically from the storage lipids of cereal grains and oilseeds?
options: Leaves contain chloroplast galactolipids rich in linolenic acid (C18:3), whereas seeds store triglycerides rich in linoleic acid
Pasture leaves store 95% saturated palmitic and stearic acid triglycerides, whereas oilseeds store only cholesterol esters
Pasture leaves contain only free volatile fatty acids, whereas cereal grains contain only non-saponifiable cuticular waxes
Both pasture leaves and oilseeds store 100% of their lipids as neutral triglycerides rich in arachidonic acid (C20:4)
explanation: Leafy green forages store lipids in chloroplast thylakoid membranes as mono- and digalactosyldiacylglycerols (galactolipids) in which $\alpha$-linolenic acid ($C18:3\text{ }n-3$) makes up 60–75% of fatty acids. Conversely, seeds and grains store neutral triglycerides rich in linoleic ($C18:2\text{ }n-6$) and oleic ($C18:1$) acids.

topic: Principles of Nutrition, Proximate Analysis & Nutrient Metabolism
questionText: What two sequential microbial steps in the rumen convert unsaturated dietary plant lipids into the hard, stearic acid-rich ($C18:0$) depot fat characteristic of ruminant tallow?
options: Beta-oxidation of intact triglycerides into acetyl-CoA in rumen fluid, followed by de novo resynthesis of stearic acid by entodiniomorph protozoa
Saponification of unsaturated triglycerides with ruminal ammonia into insoluble ammonium soaps that isomerize spontaneously into stearic acid
Lipolysis by bacterial lipases (Anaerovibrio lipolytica) releasing free fatty acids, followed by biohydrogenation by Butyrivibrio fibrisolvens
Portal absorption of intact linoleic acid triglycerides across the rumen wall, followed by enzymatic hydrogenation inside hepatic mitochondria
explanation: First, microbial lipases (`Anaerovibrio lipolytica`, `Butyrivibrio`) hydrolyze ester linkages in galactolipids and triglycerides to release free fatty acids (FFAs). Second, because a free $-COOH$ group is strictly required for isomerase/reductase action, `Butyrivibrio fibrisolvens` and related bacteria biohydrogenate C18:3 and C18:2 into saturated stearic acid (C18:0).

topic: Principles of Nutrition, Proximate Analysis & Nutrient Metabolism
questionText: During the normal ruminal biohydrogenation of linoleic acid ($cis-9, cis-12\text{ }C_{18:2}$), which health-promoting intermediate is formed first by linoleate isomerase and is also synthesized endogenously in the mammary gland from vaccenic acid ($trans-11\text{ }C_{18:1}$) via $\Delta^9$-desaturase?
options: $cis-9, trans-11$ Conjugated Linoleic Acid (rumenic acid), the major anticarcinogenic CLA in milk
Erucic acid ($cis-13\text{ }C_{22:1}$), the characteristic monounsaturated fatty acid of mustard oil
$trans-10, cis-12$ Conjugated Linoleic Acid, which potently inhibits mammary de novo lipogenesis
Arachidonic acid ($cis-5,8,11,14\text{ }C_{20:4}$), the direct precursor of series-2 prostaglandins
explanation: In the normal ruminal biohydrogenation pathway of linoleic acid, linoleate isomerase first produces $cis-9, trans-11\text{ CLA}$ (rumenic acid), which is then reduced to vaccenic acid ($trans-11\text{ }C_{18:1}$) and finally stearic acid ($C_{18:0}$). Over 70% of milk fat $cis-9, trans-11\text{ CLA}$ is synthesized in the mammary gland from absorbed vaccenic acid by stearoyl-CoA ($\Delta^9$) desaturase.

topic: Principles of Nutrition, Proximate Analysis & Nutrient Metabolism
questionText: According to the biohydrogenation theory of Milk Fat Depression (MFD) in dairy cows fed high-grain, low-roughage diets containing polyunsaturated oils, which specific ruminal intermediate downregulates mammary lipogenic enzymes?
options: Saturated palmitic acid ($C_{16:0}$) and stearic acid ($C_{18:0}$) absorbed via intestinal chylomicrons
$trans-10, cis-12$ Conjugated Linoleic Acid (CLA) formed via an altered low-pH biohydrogenation pathway
$cis-9, trans-11$ Conjugated Linoleic Acid (rumenic acid) and $trans-11\text{ }C_{18:1}$ (vaccenic acid)
Butyric acid ($C_{4:0}$) and beta-hydroxybutyric acid produced by ruminal epithelial ketogenesis
explanation: When ruminal pH drops on high-concentrate diets supplemented with unsaturated oils, bacterial isomerization shifts from the $trans-11$ pathway to the $trans-10$ pathway, forming $trans-10, cis-12\text{ CLA}$. Absorbed $trans-10, cis-12\text{ CLA}$ potently inhibits mammary SREBP-1c, acetyl-CoA carboxylase, and fatty acid synthase, causing Milk Fat Depression.

topic: Principles of Nutrition, Proximate Analysis & Nutrient Metabolism
questionText: Why must unprotected dietary fat (Ether Extract) generally be limited to no more than 5–6% of total Dry Matter in ruminant rations?
options: Dietary lipids above 6% DM chelate all ruminal potassium and sodium ions, inducing hypokalemic muscular paralysis
Ruminants lack pancreatic colipase and bile salts in the duodenum and cannot emulsify more than 50 g of lipid daily
Triglycerides above 5% DM are fermented instantly into D-lactic acid by Streptococcus bovis, causing acute acidosis
Free unsaturated fatty acids coat fiber particles and exert membrane toxicity on Gram-positive cellulolytic bacteria
explanation: Exceeding 5–6% unprotected fat in ruminant DM depresses fiber digestibility and methane production because free polyunsaturated fatty acids physically coat fiber particles, form insoluble Ca/Mg soaps, and disrupt the cell membranes of Gram-positive cellulolytic bacteria and protozoa.

topic: Principles of Nutrition, Proximate Analysis & Nutrient Metabolism
questionText: In de novo fatty acid synthesis (lipogenesis) within adipose and mammary tissues, how do ruminants differ metabolically from monogastric animals?
options: Ruminants use Acetate (and BHBA in udder) as the main carbon source and generate NADPH via NADP-isocitrate dehydrogenase
Ruminants lack acetyl-CoA carboxylase in adipocytes and can only deposit preformed dietary fatty acids absorbed via lymphatics
Ruminants utilize blood Glucose as their sole carbon precursor for lipogenesis and rely exclusively on ATP-citrate lyase and malic enzyme
Ruminants synthesize all depot and milk fatty acids exclusively inside hepatocytes using propionyl-CoA as the two-carbon primer
explanation: To spare glucose for lactose synthesis and vital tissues, ruminant adipocytes and mammary cells have very low ATP-citrate lyase and NADP-malic enzyme activity. Instead, they use ruminal Acetate ($C_2$, plus $\beta$-hydroxybutyrate in the udder) as their carbon source and generate cytosolic NADPH via the pentose phosphate pathway and cytosolic NADP-isocitrate dehydrogenase.

topic: Principles of Nutrition, Proximate Analysis & Nutrient Metabolism
questionText: Deamination and decarboxylation of the branched-chain amino acids Valine, Leucine, and Isoleucine in the rumen yield which essential growth factors required by cellulolytic bacteria (`Ruminococcus` and `Fibrobacter`)?
options: Straight-chain volatile fatty acids: formic acid, propionic acid, and n-butyric acid
Dicarboxylic organic acids: oxalic acid, succinic acid, fumaric acid, and malic acid
Branched-chain volatile fatty acids: isobutyric, isovaleric, and 2-methylbutyric acids
Aromatic phenolic acids: ferulic acid, p-coumaric acid, sinapic acid, and benzoic acid
explanation: Ruminal oxidative deamination of Valine, Leucine, and Isoleucine yields the branched-chain VFAs (iso-acids): Isobutyric acid, Isovaleric acid, and 2-Methylbutyric acid, respectively. Cellulolytic bacteria require these iso-acids to synthesize branched-chain amino acids and membrane lipids via reductive carboxylation.

topic: Principles of Nutrition, Proximate Analysis & Nutrient Metabolism
questionText: In the Hepato-Ruminal Nitrogen Cycle (Urea Recycling) of ruminants consuming low-protein roughages, how does hepatic urea re-enter the rumen to support microbial protein synthesis?
options: Endogenous skeletal muscle myosin is secreted directly through the parotid salivary duct into the oral cavity during cud chewing
Urea is actively pumped into the gall bladder and secreted with bile acids into the ileum for absorption as intact urea
Ruminal protozoa fix atmospheric nitrogen gas ($N_2$) swallowed during eructation using a molybdenum nitrogenase complex
Blood urea enters the rumen via saliva and direct diffusion across the rumen wall, where bacterial urease cleaves it to $NH_3$
explanation: In ruminants on low-N diets, renal urea excretion drops markedly and Blood Urea Nitrogen (BUN) re-enters the rumen via saliva and facilitated diffusion (UT-B transporters) across the rumen wall. Epimural bacterial urease immediately hydrolyzes urea to $2NH_3 + CO_2$, maintaining a gradient for microbial protein synthesis.

topic: Principles of Nutrition, Proximate Analysis & Nutrient Metabolism
questionText: Approximately 15–20% of total nitrogen in ruminal bacteria consists of nucleic acids (RNA and DNA). Which urinary metabolite of absorbed microbial purines is measured non-invasively to estimate ruminal Microbial Crude Protein (MCP) supply in cattle?
options: Hippuric acid formed by hepatic conjugation of benzoic acid with glycine
Allantoin (along with uric acid, xanthine, and hypoxanthine derivatives)
3-Methylhistidine released during myofibrillar actin and myosin turnover
Creatinine excreted at a constant rate per kilogram of skeletal muscle mass
explanation: Microbial nucleic acids are digested in the small intestine; absorbed purine bases are oxidized by intestinal and hepatic xanthine oxidase into Allantoin (which accounts for 80–85% of urinary purine derivatives in cattle) and uric acid. Daily urinary purine derivative excretion provides an accurate non-invasive index of ruminal MCP flow.

topic: Principles of Nutrition, Proximate Analysis & Nutrient Metabolism
questionText: Which reflex mechanism allows liquid milk sucked by a newborn calf or lamb to bypass the developing reticulorumen and flow directly from the cardia into the abomasum?
options: Secretion of concentrated hydrochloric acid (pH 1.0) inside the dorsal sac of the rumen during the first four weeks of life
Peristaltic retrograde contraction of the duodenum that pumps colostrum directly into the fundic region of the abomasum
Closure of the reticular (esophageal) groove mediated by vagal stimulation from suckling and pharyngeal chemoreceptors
Anatomical occlusion of the reticulo-ruminal fold by a congenital fibrous membrane that ruptures only when roughage is eaten
explanation: Suckling and chemical stimulation of pharyngeal receptors (by milk proteins, sodium salts in calves, and copper salts in lambs) trigger vagal efferent impulses that contract the muscular lips of the reticular (esophageal) groove into a closed tube, shunting milk directly from the cardia to the abomasum.

topic: Principles of Nutrition, Proximate Analysis & Nutrient Metabolism
questionText: In the abomasum of the suckling preruminant calf, which proteolytic enzyme predominates at pH 5.0–6.0 and specifically cleaves the $Phe_{105}-Met_{106}$ bond of $\kappa$-casein to coagulate milk into a firm calcium paracaseinate curd?
options: Carboxypeptidase A secreted as a zinc metalloenzyme into the duodenal lumen
Chymosin (Rennin) secreted as prochymosin by chief cells of the abomasum
Elastase secreted by the gastric cardiac glands in the presence of bile salts
Trypsin activated from pancreatic trypsinogen by brush-border enterokinase
explanation: In preruminant calves, abomasal chief cells secrete prochymosin (activated to Chymosin/Rennin), which exhibits high milk-clotting activity at pH 5.0–6.0. Chymosin cleaves $\kappa$-casein at $Phe_{105}-Met_{106}$ to release glycomacropeptide, allowing para-$\kappa$-casein to clot with $Ca^{2+}$ and slow gastric emptying.

topic: Principles of Nutrition, Proximate Analysis & Nutrient Metabolism
questionText: Why is Arginine a strictly essential dietary amino acid in domestic poultry (chickens and turkeys), whereas adult mammals can synthesize arginine endogenously?
options: Avian hepatocytes convert all intracellular ornithine directly into taurine and glycine for bile salt conjugation
Poultry kidneys excrete intact arginine at ten times the glomerular filtration rate of inulin and uric acid
Avian enterocytes oxidize 100% of dietary glutamate into methane before it can enter the portal circulation
Birds are uricotelic and lack hepatic Carbamoyl Phosphate Synthetase I (CPS-I) and a functional urea cycle
explanation: Mammals synthesize arginine as an intermediate of the hepatic Krebs-Henseleit urea cycle. Because birds are uricotelic and lack mitochondrial Carbamoyl Phosphate Synthetase I (CPS-I), ornithine transcarbamylase, and a functional urea cycle, poultry cannot synthesize ornithine/citrulline/arginine de novo and require dietary Arginine.

topic: Principles of Nutrition, Proximate Analysis & Nutrient Metabolism
questionText: Which two pairs of amino acids exhibit a unidirectional 'sparing effect' in animal nutrition, where the non-essential product can satisfy up to ~50% of the total requirement for its essential precursor?
options: Cystine spares Methionine, and Tyrosine spares Phenylalanine (because their synthesis from the precursor is irreversible)
Arginine spares Histidine, and Glycine spares Valine (because avian kidneys interconvert basic and branched amino acids)
Methionine spares Lysine, and Tryptophan spares Threonine (because transmethylation converts lysine into methionine)
Leucine spares Isoleucine, and Proline spares Tryptophan (because ruminal protozoa isomerize branched carbon skeletons)
explanation: Animals synthesize Cysteine/Cystine irreversibly from essential Methionine, and synthesize Tyrosine irreversibly from essential Phenylalanine (via phenylalanine hydroxylase). Providing adequate dietary Cystine or Tyrosine spares the conversion of Methionine or Phenylalanine, fulfilling up to ~50% of the Total Sulfur Amino Acid (Met+Cys) or Aromatic Amino Acid (Phe+Tyr) requirement.

topic: Principles of Nutrition, Proximate Analysis & Nutrient Metabolism
questionText: When the 20 standard amino acids are classified by the metabolic fate of their carbon skeletons after deamination, which two amino acids are strictly ketogenic (incapable of contributing net carbon to gluconeogenesis)?
options: Alanine and Serine, which are transaminated directly to pyruvate in the liver
Leucine and Lysine, which degrade exclusively to acetyl-CoA and acetoacetate
Valine and Methionine, which enter the TCA cycle via propionyl-CoA and succinyl-CoA
Glutamate and Aspartate, which enter the TCA cycle as alpha-ketoglutarate and oxaloacetate
explanation: Leucine and Lysine are the ONLY two strictly ketogenic amino acids in mammalian metabolism; their carbon skeletons yield only acetyl-CoA and acetoacetyl-CoA/acetoacetate, which cannot produce net glucose. Isoleucine, Phenylalanine, Tryptophan, and Tyrosine are both glucogenic and ketogenic, while the other 14 are strictly glucogenic.

topic: Feed Evaluation & Energy/Protein Partitioning (TDN, ME, NE, RUP/RDP)
questionText: In a conventional in vivo total fecal collection digestibility trial using adult cattle or buffaloes, why is a 10 to 14-day preliminary adaptation period mandatory before the 7-day collection phase?
options: To clear prior ration residues from the gut and allow the ruminal microbial population to stabilize on the test diet
To deplete endogenous hepatic glycogen and adipose stores so that metabolic fecal nitrogen excretion falls to zero
To induce complete defaunation of ruminal holotrich protozoa so that only bacterial cellulase activity is measured during collection
To allow complete closure of the reticular groove so that test roughages pass directly into the abomasum without fermentation
explanation: Because ruminants have a large reticuloruminal volume and slow digesta passage (mean retention time 40–70 hours), a 10–14 day preliminary period is required to flush out prior rations, establish steady-state feed intake, and adapt the rumen microbiome before a 7–10 day total fecal collection.

topic: Feed Evaluation & Energy/Protein Partitioning (TDN, ME, NE, RUP/RDP)
questionText: Why is the 'Apparent Digestibility' of Crude Protein always lower than its 'True Digestibility' in a conventional feeding trial?
options: Urinary urea and allantoin are accidentally mixed with feces inside standard metabolism stalls during total collection
Ruminal ammonia absorbed across the rumen wall is excluded from the Kjeldahl nitrogen assay of the offered diet
Feces contain endogenous Metabolic Fecal Nitrogen from sloughed mucosal cells, digestive enzymes, and bacteria
Volatile fatty acids produced from amino acid deamination evaporate from the fecal drying oven at 65°C
explanation: Apparent digestibility underestimates true digestibility because feces contain endogenous Metabolic Fecal Nitrogen (MFN: sloughed mucosal cells, mucoproteins, spent digestive enzymes, and undigested microbial debris). In ruminants, MFN averages ~5 g N (or ~30–31 g CP) per kg of fecal dry matter.

topic: Feed Evaluation & Energy/Protein Partitioning (TDN, ME, NE, RUP/RDP)
questionText: How is the digestibility coefficient of a high-energy concentrate (such as maize grain or groundnut cake) determined in ruminants, given that feeding 100% concentrate alone causes fatal ruminal acidosis?
options: By boiling the concentrate in 1.25% sulfuric acid and assuming 100% of the soluble filtrate is digested in vivo
By infusing the ground concentrate directly into the ileum through a T-cannula to bypass ruminal fermentation completely
By fasting the bullock for 7 days prior to feeding a single 500 g bolus of the test concentrate mixed with chromic oxide
By the digestibility-by-difference method using a known basal roughage ration substituted with 20–30% concentrate
explanation: Concentrates and protein supplements cannot be fed as the sole diet to ruminants because they require minimum roughage fiber for rumination. Therefore, a basal roughage is evaluated in Period 1, and the test concentrate is added to the basal roughage in Period 2; concentrate digestibility is calculated by difference.

topic: Feed Evaluation & Energy/Protein Partitioning (TDN, ME, NE, RUP/RDP)
questionText: In pasture grazing studies where total fecal collection is impractical, which pair of internal (natural) and external (dosed) inert markers is classically used to determine dry matter digestibility and fecal output?
options: Dietary urea ($CO(NH_2)_2$) as the internal marker and vital methylene blue dye as the external marker
Soluble citrus pectin as the internal marker and anionic sodium lauryl sulfate detergent as the external marker
Acid-Insoluble Ash (AIA) as the internal marker and Chromic oxide ($Cr_2O_3$) as the external marker
Gelatinized amylose starch as the internal marker and heptahydrate ferrous sulfate ($FeSO_4$) as the external marker
explanation: Internal markers are natural indigestible components of the feed (Acid-Insoluble Ash AIA, Acid Detergent Lignin ADL, indigestible NDF, or odd-chain plant cuticular wax n-alkanes $C_{31}/C_{33}$) used to estimate digestibility%, whereas external markers (Chromic oxide $Cr_2O_3$, Titanium dioxide $TiO_2$, Ytterbium, or even-chain $C_{32}$ alkane) are dosed in known daily gram amounts to estimate total fecal output.

topic: Feed Evaluation & Energy/Protein Partitioning (TDN, ME, NE, RUP/RDP)
questionText: When using an indigestible internal marker such as Acid-Insoluble Ash (AIA) or Lignin, which equation correctly calculates the apparent digestibility percentage of a specific nutrient ($N$)?
options: $\text{Digestibility (\%)} = 100 - \left[100 \times \frac{\%\text{Marker in Feces} - \%\text{Marker in Feed}}{\%\text{Nutrient in Feed} + \%\text{Nutrient in Feces}}\right]$
$\text{Digestibility (\%)} = \left[\frac{\%\text{Marker in Feed}}{100 \times \%\text{Nutrient in Feces}} + \frac{\%\text{Nutrient in Feed}}{100 \times \%\text{Marker in Feces}}\right] \times 100$
$\text{Digestibility (\%)} = 100 - \left[100 \times \frac{\%\text{Marker in Feces}}{\%\text{Marker in Feed}} \times \frac{\%\text{Nutrient in Feed}}{\%\text{Nutrient in Feces}}\right]$
$\text{Digestibility (\%)} = 100 - \left[100 \times \frac{\%\text{Marker in Feed}}{\%\text{Marker in Feces}} \times \frac{\%\text{Nutrient in Feces}}{\%\text{Nutrient in Feed}}\right]$
explanation: Because the total weight of an indigestible marker consumed equals the total weight excreted in feces, the ratio $(\%I_{feed} / \%I_{feces})$ equals $(DM_{feces} / DM_{feed})$. Multiplying this by $(\%N_{feces} / \%N_{feed})$ gives the fraction of nutrient excreted; subtracting from 100% yields the Nutrient Digestibility %.

topic: Feed Evaluation & Energy/Protein Partitioning (TDN, ME, NE, RUP/RDP)
questionText: A grazing cow is fed grass containing 2.0% Acid-Insoluble Ash (AIA) and 12.0% Crude Protein on a DM basis. If her feces contain 5.0% AIA and 7.5% Crude Protein on a DM basis, what are the Dry Matter Digestibility (DMD) and Crude Protein Digestibility?
options: 40.0% DMD and 62.5% Crude Protein Digestibility
60.0% DMD and 75.0% Crude Protein Digestibility
50.0% DMD and 80.0% Crude Protein Digestibility
75.0% DMD and 60.0% Crude Protein Digestibility

topic: Feed Evaluation & Energy/Protein Partitioning (TDN, ME, NE, RUP/RDP)
questionText: When measuring the fractional passage rate (outflow rate) of the liquid versus solid particulate phases of digesta from the reticulorumen, which pair of phase-specific markers is standard?
options: Cobalt-EDTA (or Cr-EDTA) for the liquid phase and Ytterbium (or Cr-mordanted fiber) for the particulate phase
Sudan III lipophilic dye for the liquid phase and water-soluble phenol red indicator for the solid particulate phase
Chromic oxide sesquioxide for the liquid phase and high-molecular-weight polyethylene glycol for the solid particulate phase
Acid detergent lignin for the liquid phase and insoluble titanium dioxide powder for the solid particulate phase
explanation: Water-soluble chelated complexes such as Cobalt-EDTA (Co-EDTA), Cr-EDTA, or high-molecular-weight Polyethylene Glycol (PEG 4000) remain strictly in solution to track liquid outflow rate ($k_l$), whereas rare-earth elements bound to fiber (Ytterbium, Cerium, Dysprosium) or Chromium-mordanted NDF track solid particulate passage rate ($k_p$).

topic: Feed Evaluation & Energy/Protein Partitioning (TDN, ME, NE, RUP/RDP)
questionText: The classic Tilley and Terry (1963) two-stage in vitro digestibility technique simulates ruminant digestion through which sequential 48-hour + 48-hour incubations at 39°C?
options: Stage 1: 48 h reflux in 1.25% dilute sulfuric acid; Stage 2: 48 h reflux in 1.25% dilute sodium hydroxide solution
Stage 1: 48 h hydrolysis in alkaline pancreatic trypsin (pH 8.0); Stage 2: 48 h aerobic incubation in strained rumen liquor
Stage 1: 48 h anaerobic incubation in rumen liquor + McDougall's buffer; Stage 2: 48 h digestion in acid-pepsin (pH 2.0)
Stage 1: 48 h digestion in acid-pepsin (0.1 N HCl, pH 2.0); Stage 2: 48 h extraction in neutral detergent sodium lauryl sulfate
explanation: Tilley and Terry (1963) devised a two-stage procedure: Stage 1 incubates 0.5 g forage anaerobically for 48 hours at 39°C with strained rumen liquor and McDougall's artificial saliva buffer (simulating rumen fermentation); Stage 2 incubates the residue for 48 hours with pepsin in dilute HCl at pH ~2.0 (simulating abomasal digestion of microbial and undegraded dietary protein) to yield Apparent In Vitro Dry Matter Digestibility (IVDMD).

topic: Feed Evaluation & Energy/Protein Partitioning (TDN, ME, NE, RUP/RDP)
questionText: In Goering and Van Soest's modification of the Tilley and Terry in vitro digestibility method, replacing the 48-hour Stage 2 acid-pepsin incubation with a 1-hour reflux in Neutral Detergent Solution yields which parameter?
options: Acid Detergent Insoluble Nitrogen (ADIN), because sodium lauryl sulfate precipitates Maillard reaction proteins
Apparent Digestible Energy (ADE), because neutral detergent extracts only volatile fatty acids and methane gas
Metabolizable Protein (MP), because neutral detergent selectively isolates undegraded dietary bypass amino acids
True In Vitro Dry Matter Digestibility (True IVDMD), as neutral detergent dissolves all residual microbial debris
explanation: Whereas Tilley & Terry's Stage 2 acid-pepsin leaves behind undigested bacterial cell walls (mimicking in vivo Apparent Digestibility), refluxing the Stage 1 fermentation residue for 1 hour in Neutral Detergent Solution dissolves all microbial matter and leaves only undigested plant NDF—measuring True IVDMD and saving 47 hours.

topic: Feed Evaluation & Energy/Protein Partitioning (TDN, ME, NE, RUP/RDP)
questionText: In the Ørskov and McDonald (1979) in situ Nylon (Dacron) bag technique used in rumen-cannulated cattle to determine protein degradability ($p = a + b(1 - e^{-ct})$), how is Effective Degradability ($ED$) calculated at a given ruminal solid outflow rate ($k$)?
options: $ED = \frac{a \times b}{c + k} \times 100$
$ED = a + \frac{b \times c}{c + k}$
$ED = (a + b) \times e^{-k \cdot t}$
$ED = a - \frac{b \times k}{c - k}$
explanation: In Ørskov and McDonald's exponential kinetics model, $a$ is the rapidly water-soluble fraction washed out at $t=0$, $b$ is the insoluble but potentially degradable fraction, $c$ is the fractional rate constant of degradation ($\text{h}^{-1}$) of fraction $b$, and $k$ is the fractional rumen outflow/passage rate ($\text{h}^{-1}$, e.g. 0.02, 0.05, or $0.08\text{ h}^{-1}$). Integrating degradation against passage gives $ED = a + \frac{b \cdot c}{c + k}$.

topic: Feed Evaluation & Energy/Protein Partitioning (TDN, ME, NE, RUP/RDP)
questionText: A soybean meal sample evaluated by the in situ nylon bag method has a soluble fraction $a = 20\%$, a potentially degradable insoluble fraction $b = 75\%$, and a degradation rate constant $c = 0.08\text{ h}^{-1}$. If the rumen solid outflow rate in a high-yielding dairy cow is $k = 0.04\text{ h}^{-1}$, what are the Effective Degradability (RDP%) and Bypass Protein (RUP%) percentages of its Crude Protein?
options: 70% RDP and 30% RUP
50% RDP and 50% RUP
75% RDP and 25% RUP
60% RDP and 40% RUP
explanation: Using $ED = a + \frac{b \times c}{c + k}$: $ED = 20 + \frac{75 \times 0.08}{0.08 + 0.04} = 20 + \frac{6.0}{0.12} = 20 + 50 = 70\%$. Therefore, Rumen Degradable Protein (RDP) is 70% of CP, and Rumen Undegradable / Bypass Protein ($RUP = 100 - RDP$) is $30\%$ of CP.

topic: Feed Evaluation & Energy/Protein Partitioning (TDN, ME, NE, RUP/RDP)
questionText: In the Hohenheim Gas Production Test (Menke and Steingass, 1988) for predicting the Metabolizable Energy (ME) of ruminant feeds, what sample size and apparatus are incubated at 39°C?
options: 200 mg of milled feed incubated with 30 mL buffered rumen liquor in 100 mL calibrated glass syringes for 24 hours
5 g of dry feed suspended in 40-micron polyester bags inside the ventral rumen sac of a fistulated buffalo for 72 hours
50 g of intact forage incubated in 5-liter polyethylene carboys filled with 0.1 N hydrochloric acid for 96 hours
10 g of pelleted concentrate boiled in 500 mL Soxhlet flasks containing petroleum ether and sodium sulfite for 6 hours
explanation: In the Menke & Steingass (1988) Hohenheim Gas Test, 200 mg of 1-mm ground feed DM is incubated anaerobically with 30 mL of a 1:2 mixture of strained rumen fluid and bicarbonate-mineral buffer inside lubricated 100 mL calibrated glass syringes on a rotor at 39°C; 24-hour net gas volume ($CO_2 + CH_4$, mL/200 mg DM) combined with CP and EE accurately predicts OMD and ME.

topic: Feed Evaluation & Energy/Protein Partitioning (TDN, ME, NE, RUP/RDP)
questionText: A compounded cattle ration contains 15% Digestible Crude Protein (DCP), 12% Digestible Crude Fiber (DCF), 40% Digestible Nitrogen-Free Extract (DNFE), 4% Digestible Ether Extract (DEE), and 8% Total Ash on a DM basis. What is its Total Digestible Nutrients (TDN) percentage?
options: 67.0% TDN on a dry matter basis
84.0% TDN on a dry matter basis
76.0% TDN on a dry matter basis
71.0% TDN on a dry matter basis
explanation: $\text{TDN (\%)} = \%DCP + \%DCF + \%DNFE + (\%DEE \times 2.25)$. Substituting the values: $TDN = 15 + 12 + 40 + (4 \times 2.25) = 67 + 9.0 = 76.0\%$ (Total Ash yields no energy and is excluded).

topic: Feed Evaluation & Energy/Protein Partitioning (TDN, ME, NE, RUP/RDP)
questionText: What is the major mechanistic limitation of the Total Digestible Nutrients (TDN) system when comparing fibrous roughages (such as wheat straw) with cereal concentrates (such as maize grain) for productive functions like lactation or fattening?
options: TDN multiplies Digestible Crude Fiber by 2.25 instead of 1.0, artificially doubling the apparent energy content of cereal grains
TDN accounts only for fecal losses and ignores methane and heat increment losses, which are higher for roughages
TDN measures energy in megajoules of net energy rather than digestible organic matter, making it inapplicable to growing calves
TDN deducts urinary urea energy twice, which severely underestimates the net caloric value of high-protein oilseed cakes
explanation: TDN is fundamentally a measure of Digestible Energy (1 kg TDN $\approx 4.4\text{ Mcal DE}$ or $3.6\text{ Mcal ME}$) and considers only fecal losses. Because fibrous roughages suffer much higher methane losses and generate a much larger Heat Increment (HI) of fermentation and acetate metabolism than concentrates, 1 kg of TDN from straw yields far less Net Energy ($NE$) than 1 kg of TDN from maize.

topic: Feed Evaluation & Energy/Protein Partitioning (TDN, ME, NE, RUP/RDP)
questionText: When pure nutrients are completely combusted at 25–30 atmospheres of oxygen in an adiabatic Bomb Calorimeter (calibrated with benzoic acid at 6.318 kcal/g), what are the average Gross Energy (GE) values per gram of carbohydrate, protein, and lipid?
options: 5.65 kcal/g for carbohydrate, 4.15 kcal/g for protein, and 7.45 kcal/g for lipid
4.00 kcal/g for carbohydrate, 4.00 kcal/g for protein, and 9.00 kcal/g for lipid
3.49 kcal/g for carbohydrate, 4.96 kcal/g for protein, and 5.95 kcal/g for lipid
4.15 kcal/g for carbohydrate, 5.65 kcal/g for protein, and 9.40 kcal/g for lipid
explanation: In bomb calorimetry, average heats of combustion (Gross Energy) are: Carbohydrates ~4.15 kcal/g (glucose 3.74, starch/cellulose 4.18–4.20), Proteins ~5.65 kcal/g (because N is oxidized to oxides of nitrogen in the bomb), and Fats/Lipids ~9.40–9.45 kcal/g (whereas 4-4-9 kcal/g are Atwater physiological fuel values for humans).

topic: Feed Evaluation & Energy/Protein Partitioning (TDN, ME, NE, RUP/RDP)
questionText: Why is the physiological Metabolizable Energy of 1 gram of pure digested protein (~4.3 kcal/g) substantially lower than its Bomb Calorimeter Gross Energy (5.65 kcal/g)?
options: Peptide bond synthesis in the ribosome consumes 1.35 kcal of heat per gram of dietary protein ingested
Protein carbon skeletons cannot enter the mitochondrial tricarboxylic acid cycle in domestic mammals
Animals cannot oxidize protein nitrogen completely and must excrete energy-containing urea or uric acid in urine
Proteins are only 50% digestible in the mammalian small intestine due to trypsin inhibitor binding
explanation: In a bomb calorimeter, protein nitrogen is oxidized completely to $N_2 / HNO_3$, releasing 5.65 kcal/g. In the animal body, nitrogen cannot be oxidized and must be excreted as energy-rich urea in mammals (losing ~1.25 kcal/g protein, or 5.4 kcal/g urinary N) or uric acid in birds (losing ~8.22 kcal/g urinary N).

topic: Feed Evaluation & Energy/Protein Partitioning (TDN, ME, NE, RUP/RDP)
questionText: In quantitative ruminant energetics (ARC / NRC / ICAR), what is the standard conversion factor used to estimate Metabolizable Energy (ME) from Digestible Energy (DE), and what is the caloric equivalent of 1 kg of TDN?
options: $ME = 0.50 \times DE$; and 1 kg of TDN is equivalent to 2.20 Mcal of Digestible Energy
$ME = 0.82 \times DE$; and 1 kg of TDN is equivalent to 4.40 Mcal of Digestible Energy
$ME = 1.25 \times DE$; and 1 kg of TDN is equivalent to 5.65 Mcal of Digestible Energy
$ME = 0.96 \times DE$; and 1 kg of TDN is equivalent to 9.40 Mcal of Digestible Energy
explanation: In ruminants, approximately 18% of Digestible Energy is lost in urine (~8–10% of DE) and eructated methane (~8–10% of DE, or 6–8% of GE), giving the classic NRC relationship $ME = 0.82 \times DE$. One kilogram of TDN provides approximately 4.4 Mcal (4400 kcal) of DE and $4.4 \times 0.82 \approx 3.6\text{ Mcal}$ (15.1 MJ) of ME.

topic: Feed Evaluation & Energy/Protein Partitioning (TDN, ME, NE, RUP/RDP)
questionText: In poultry bioenergetics, Apparent Metabolizable Energy is routinely corrected to zero nitrogen balance ($AME_n$). Why is a correction factor of 8.22 kcal subtracted per gram of nitrogen retained in the bird's body?
options: 8.22 kcal is the Gross Energy of uric acid excreted per gram of nitrogen when tissue protein is catabolized
8.22 kcal is the heat of fermentation released by cecal bacteria per gram of dietary uric acid
8.22 kcal is the mechanical energy required by the avian gizzard to grind 1 gram of soybean meal protein
8.22 kcal is the bomb calorimeter combustion energy value of 1 gram of feather keratin shed in poultry excreta
explanation: Growing chicks retain more dietary nitrogen as body protein than adult roosters, so growing birds excrete less energy-containing uric acid in droppings per gram of feed eaten. To standardize ME values across birds of different growth rates, $AME$ is corrected to zero N retention ($AME_n$) by subtracting 8.22 kcal (the combustion energy of uric acid containing 1 g of N) per gram of N retained.

topic: Feed Evaluation & Energy/Protein Partitioning (TDN, ME, NE, RUP/RDP)
questionText: Under which environmental temperature condition does the Heat Increment (HI) of feeding actually become part of the useful Net Energy of the ration rather than a waste heat loss?
options: When the animal is fasting inside an adiabatic respiration calorimeter chamber maintained at 28°C
When the ambient temperature exceeds the Upper Critical Temperature during severe summer heat stress
When the animal is maintained strictly within the Thermoneutral Zone at 60% ambient relative humidity
When the ambient temperature falls below the Lower Critical Temperature, sparing tissue oxidation for warmth
explanation: Within or above the Thermoneutral Zone, Heat Increment (HI: heat of ruminal fermentation + heat of nutrient metabolism/SDA) must be dissipated to the environment and is wasted. However, when ambient temperature drops below the Lower Critical Temperature (LCT), HI helps maintain core body temperature, sparing Net Energy! Hence high-roughage diets (high HI) help keep ruminants warm in winter.

topic: Feed Evaluation & Energy/Protein Partitioning (TDN, ME, NE, RUP/RDP)
questionText: When comparing the partial efficiency ($k$) of utilization of Metabolizable Energy (ME) for different physiological functions in dairy cattle, which order of efficiency is correct?
options: Efficiency for fetal pregnancy growth ($k_c$) > Efficiency for maintenance ($k_m$) > Efficiency for lactation ($k_l$)
Efficiency for maintenance ($k_m$) > Efficiency for lactation ($k_l$) > Efficiency for body tissue gain ($k_g$)
Efficiency for wool fiber growth ($k_w$) > Efficiency for maintenance ($k_m$) > Efficiency for milk synthesis ($k_l$)
Efficiency for body fat deposition ($k_f$) > Efficiency for milk synthesis ($k_l$) > Efficiency for maintenance ($k_m$)
explanation: Metabolizable Energy is utilized most efficiently for Maintenance ($k_m \approx 0.68-0.75$, where ATP directly replaces tissue turnover), followed closely by Lactation ($k_l \approx 0.60-0.65$), whereas body tissue Gain/Fattening in growing/finishing ruminants is notably lower ($k_g / k_f \approx 0.35-0.50$, especially on high-forage diets), and conceptus/pregnancy efficiency is lowest ($k_c \approx 0.13-0.15$).

topic: Feed Evaluation & Energy/Protein Partitioning (TDN, ME, NE, RUP/RDP)
questionText: In the NRC Net Energy system for lactating dairy cows developed by Moe and Tyrrell at Beltsville, why are feed energy values and cow requirements for BOTH maintenance and milk production expressed in a single unit ($NE_L$, Mcal/kg)?
options: Because the partial efficiencies of ME utilization for maintenance ($k_m$) and lactation ($k_l$) are nearly equal
Because ruminal methane production ceases completely during peak lactation in high-yielding Holstein cows
Because Lofgreen and Garrett proved that body fat mobilization during early lactation occurs at 100% thermodynamic efficiency
Because lactating dairy cows have zero maintenance energy requirement once daily milk yield exceeds 15 kg of 4% FCM
explanation: While beef cattle use the California Net Energy System (Lofgreen & Garrett, 1968) with two separate values ($NE_m$ and $NE_g$) because $k_m$ and $k_g$ diverge widely, Moe and Tyrrell showed that in dairy cows the energetic efficiencies of maintenance ($k_m$) and milk synthesis ($k_l$) are very close (~62–65%), allowing both maintenance and production to be combined into a single unit: Net Energy for Lactation ($NE_L$).

topic: Feed Evaluation & Energy/Protein Partitioning (TDN, ME, NE, RUP/RDP)
questionText: In Oskar Kellner's classical 'Starch Equivalent' (SE) system of net energy evaluation in fattening steers, 1 kg of digestible starch deposited 236 g of body fat (1.00 SE). What are Kellner's pure nutrient SE factors for 1 kg of digestible true protein and 1 kg of digestible oilseed fat, respectively?
options: 0.70 SE for digestible true protein and 3.50 SE for digestible oilseed fat
1.00 SE for digestible true protein and 1.91 SE for digestible oilseed fat
1.25 SE for digestible true protein and 2.25 SE for digestible oilseed fat
0.94 SE for digestible true protein and 2.41 SE for digestible oilseed fat
explanation: In Kellner's respiration experiments with fattening oxen, 1 kg of digestible starch produced 236 g of body fat (assigned SE = 1.00). Relative to starch, 1 kg of digestible true protein produced 222 g fat (SE factor = 0.94), digestible fat from coarse roughages gave SE = 1.91, fat from cereal grains gave SE = 2.12, and fat from oilseeds/oilcakes gave SE = 2.41.

topic: Feed Evaluation & Energy/Protein Partitioning (TDN, ME, NE, RUP/RDP)
questionText: In indirect respiration calorimetry, how is the Respiratory Quotient (RQ) defined, and what are the characteristic RQ values for the complete oxidation of pure carbohydrate, mixed protein, and pure fat (tripalmitin)?
options: $RQ = \text{moles } O_2\text{ consumed} / \text{moles } CO_2\text{ produced}$; Carbohydrate = 0.70, Protein = 0.80, Fat = 1.00
$RQ = \text{liters } CH_4\text{ eructated} / \text{liters } O_2\text{ consumed}$; Carbohydrate = 1.25, Protein = 1.00, Fat = 0.50
$RQ = \text{moles } CO_2\text{ produced} / \text{moles } O_2\text{ consumed}$; Carbohydrate = 1.00, Protein = 0.80, Fat = 0.70
$RQ = \text{grams } H_2O\text{ vaporized} / \text{liters } CO_2\text{ produced}$; Carbohydrate = 0.85, Protein = 0.94, Fat = 0.60
explanation: $RQ = \frac{\text{Volume (or moles) of } CO_2\text{ produced}}{\text{Volume (or moles) of } O_2\text{ consumed}}$. For carbohydrates ($C_6H_{12}O_6 + 6O_2 \to 6CO_2 + 6H_2O$), $RQ = 6/6 = 1.00$. For fats (e.g., tripalmitin $2C_{51}H_{98}O_6 + 145O_2 \to 102CO_2 + 98H_2O$), $RQ = 102/145 = 0.703$. For mixed protein oxidized to urea, $RQ \approx 0.80-0.82$.

topic: Feed Evaluation & Energy/Protein Partitioning (TDN, ME, NE, RUP/RDP)
questionText: What physiological or metabolic state is indicated when a non-ruminant animal in a respiration chamber exhibits a non-protein Respiratory Quotient (RQ) significantly greater than 1.0 (e.g., RQ = 1.25 to 1.35)?
options: Severe starvation accompanied by rapid mobilization and ketogenesis of adipose depot triglycerides
Exclusive oxidation of dietary branched-chain amino acids following a high-casein meal
Active de novo lipogenesis converting oxygen-rich dietary carbohydrate into oxygen-poor body fat
Diabetic ketoacidosis with hyperventilation and complete blockade of cellular glucose uptake
explanation: When an animal (such as a finishing pig or force-fed goose) is synthesizing oxygen-poor fatty acids ($C_{16}H_{32}O_2$) from oxygen-rich carbohydrates ($C_6H_{12}O_6$), surplus intramolecular oxygen from glucose spares inhaled $O_2$ while decarboxylation of pyruvate to acetyl-CoA releases abundant $CO_2$, driving the $RQ$ above 1.0.

topic: Feed Evaluation & Energy/Protein Partitioning (TDN, ME, NE, RUP/RDP)
questionText: In open-circuit indirect respiration calorimetry of ruminants, Brouwer's (1965) classic equation calculates total daily Heat Production (HP, kcal) from which four measured parameters?
options: Kilograms of Dry Matter intake, liters of drinking water, kilograms of fecal dry matter, and rectal temperature
Liters of $O_2$ consumed, liters of $CO_2$ produced, liters of $CH_4$ produced, and grams of urinary $N$ excreted
Grams of digested protein, grams of digested ether extract, grams of digested crude fiber, and basal heart rate
Millimoles of ruminal acetate, propionate, and butyrate plus milligrams of urinary allantoin and uric acid excreted
explanation: Brouwer's (1965) universal indirect calorimetry equation for ruminants is: $HP\text{ (kcal)} = 3.866 \times O_2\text{ (L)} + 1.200 \times CO_2\text{ (L)} - 0.518 \times CH_4\text{ (L)} - 1.431 \times N_{urine}\text{ (g)}$, accounting for carbohydrate/fat/protein oxidation and subtracting anaerobic methane fermentation energy.

topic: Feed Evaluation & Energy/Protein Partitioning (TDN, ME, NE, RUP/RDP)
questionText: In a Carbon-Nitrogen (C-N) Balance trial conducted in a respiration chamber to determine energy retention from protein and fat deposition, what standard elemental percentages of Nitrogen and Carbon are assumed for body protein, and what percentage of Carbon is assumed for body fat?
options: Body protein contains 16.0% N and 52.0% C; body fat contains 76.5% C
Body protein contains 15.67% N and 30.0% C; body fat contains 94.0% C
Body protein contains 10.0% N and 76.5% C; body fat contains 52.0% C
Body protein contains 25.0% N and 40.0% C; body fat contains 50.0% C
explanation: In a C-N balance experiment: (1) Retained Nitrogen ($g$) $\times 6.25$ gives Retained Body Protein (since protein is 16.0% N); (2) since body protein contains 52.0% Carbon, Carbon retained in protein = $\text{Protein gained} \times 0.52$; (3) subtracting protein carbon from total retained carbon gives Carbon retained in fat; and (4) dividing fat carbon by 0.765 (since body fat is 76.5% C) yields Retained Body Fat!

topic: Feed Evaluation & Energy/Protein Partitioning (TDN, ME, NE, RUP/RDP)
questionText: During a C-N balance study, a growing steer retains 24 g of Nitrogen and 462.5 g of total Carbon per day. Using standard composition constants (protein = 16% N, 52% C; fat = 76.5% C), how many grams of body protein and body fat are deposited daily?
options: 240 g of body protein and 300 g of body fat per day
150 g of body protein and 384.5 g of body fat per day
100 g of body protein and 500 g of body fat per day
150 g of body protein and 500 g of body fat per day
explanation: Step 1: $\text{Protein retained} = 24\text{ g N} \times 6.25 = 150\text{ g protein/day}$. Step 2: $\text{Carbon in retained protein} = 150\text{ g} \times 0.52 = 78.0\text{ g C}$. Step 3: $\text{Carbon in retained fat} = 462.5 - 78.0 = 384.5\text{ g C}$. Step 4: $\text{Fat retained} = 384.5 / 0.765 = 502.6 \approx 500\text{ g fat/day}$.

topic: Feed Evaluation & Energy/Protein Partitioning (TDN, ME, NE, RUP/RDP)
questionText: How does Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR) or Fasting Heat Production scale allometrically with live body weight ($W$ in kg) across mature warm-blooded mammals of different body sizes (Kleiber's Law)?
options: Linearly with live body weight ($W^{1.0}$), averaging 70 kcal per kg of live weight per day
With the square root of body weight ($W^{0.50}$), averaging 150 kcal per metabolic unit per day
With metabolic body size ($W^{0.75}$), averaging ~70 kcal per kg $W^{0.75}$ per day
With the cube of live body weight ($W^{3.0}$), averaging 10 kcal per metabolic unit per day
explanation: Max Kleiber (1932) demonstrated that across interspecies mammals from mice to cattle, daily Fasting Heat Production (Basal Metabolic Rate) is proportional to the three-quarters power of live weight—termed Metabolic Body Size ($W^{0.75}$)— according to the equation $FHP\text{ (kcal/day)} = 70 \times W_{kg}^{0.75}$.

topic: Feed Evaluation & Energy/Protein Partitioning (TDN, ME, NE, RUP/RDP)
questionText: What does a 'Negative Nitrogen Balance' ($N_{intake} < N_{fecal} + N_{urinary}$) signify in an adult animal?
options: Complete conversion of dietary non-protein nitrogen into milk casein with zero urinary urea excretion
Accidental over-supplementation of rumen-protected methionine and lysine above the maintenance requirement
Rapid skeletal muscle hypertrophy and positive nitrogen retention during compensatory growth in feedlot steers
Catabolism of endogenous body tissue proteins exceeds dietary protein accretion, causing net nitrogen loss
explanation: Negative nitrogen balance occurs when nitrogen excretion in feces and urine exceeds nitrogen intake, indicating net breakdown of body tissue proteins (due to fasting, energy/protein malnutrition, absence of a single essential amino acid causing other amino acids to be deaminated, or catabolic illness/trauma).

topic: Feed Evaluation & Energy/Protein Partitioning (TDN, ME, NE, RUP/RDP)
questionText: In the classical Thomas-Mitchell method for determining the Biological Value (BV) of a dietary protein in monogastrics, what does Biological Value specifically measure, and how are endogenous losses corrected?
options: Geometric mean of the ten essential amino acids in the test protein relative to whole hen egg reference albumin
Percentage of truly absorbed nitrogen retained in the body after correcting for Metabolic Fecal and Endogenous Urinary N
Weight gain in grams per gram of crude protein consumed over a 28-day feeding period in weanling male rats on 10% CP
Percentage of gross dietary nitrogen absorbed across the small intestine without correcting for urinary nitrogen excretion
explanation: Biological Value (BV) is defined as the percentage of *truly absorbed* nitrogen that is retained by the body: $BV = \frac{N_I - (FN - MFN) - (UN - EUN)}{N_I - (FN - MFN)} \times 100$. Adding MFN (measured on a protein-free diet) in the denominator gives truly absorbed N, while adding both MFN and EUN in the numerator accounts for nitrogen used to replace obligatory endogenous wear-and-tear.

topic: Feed Evaluation & Energy/Protein Partitioning (TDN, ME, NE, RUP/RDP)
questionText: In a nitrogen balance trial on a growing pig, daily Nitrogen Intake ($N_I$) is 25.0 g, Fecal Nitrogen ($FN$) is 7.0 g, Metabolic Fecal Nitrogen ($MFN$) is 2.0 g, Urinary Nitrogen ($UN$) is 9.0 g, and Endogenous Urinary Nitrogen ($EUN$) is 3.0 g. What is the Thomas-Mitchell Biological Value (BV) of the diet?
options: 70.0% Biological Value
80.0% Biological Value
60.0% Biological Value
50.0% Biological Value
explanation: $\text{Truly Absorbed N} = N_I - (FN - MFN) = 25.0 - (7.0 - 2.0) = 20.0\text{ g/day}$. $\text{Truly Retained N} = \text{Absorbed N} - (UN - EUN) = 20.0 - (9.0 - 3.0) = 20.0 - 6.0 = 14.0\text{ g/day}$. Therefore, $BV = (14.0 / 20.0) \times 100 = 70.0\%$.

topic: Feed Evaluation & Energy/Protein Partitioning (TDN, ME, NE, RUP/RDP)
questionText: How does 'Net Protein Utilization' (NPU, Miller and Bender) differ mathematically from 'Biological Value' (BV)?
options: $NPU = \frac{\text{BV} \times \text{True Digestibility}}{100} = \frac{\text{Truly Retained N}}{\text{Total N Intake}} \times 100$
$NPU = \text{BV} + \text{Apparent Digestibility}$, always yielding a numerical value higher than Biological Value
$NPU = \text{BV} / \text{True Digestibility}$, expressing retained nitrogen per unit of metabolic body weight ($W^{0.75}$)
$NPU = \text{Weight Gain (g)} / \text{Protein Intake (g)}$, ignoring both fecal and urinary nitrogen losses
explanation: Whereas Biological Value (BV) measures retained N as a percentage of *absorbed* N (ignoring how poorly digestible the protein might be), Net Protein Utilization (NPU) measures retained N as a percentage of *total ingested* N: $NPU = \frac{BV \times \text{True Digestibility}}{100}$. Thus, a heat-damaged protein with low digestibility will have a much lower NPU than BV.

topic: Feed Evaluation & Energy/Protein Partitioning (TDN, ME, NE, RUP/RDP)
questionText: Which biological assay evaluates protein quality simply as the ratio of body weight gain (in grams) to total crude protein consumed (in grams) over a 28-day trial using weanling male rats fed a diet containing 10% test protein?
options: Essential Amino Acid Index (EAAI) developed by Oser using geometric means
Chemical Score (CS) developed by Block and Mitchell using whole egg protein
Protein Efficiency Ratio (PER) developed by Osborne, Mendel, and Ferry
Gross Protein Value (GPV) developed by Heiman and Carver in growing chicks
